The 6 Slowest Lamborghinis Ever Built Are Also Some of the Coolest
28 photos
Photo: Lamborghini
There are a few car brands out there that started out from a vengeance, and Lamborghini is probably the best known in that category. To be more precise, Lamborghini only exists as a supercar maker because of an argument about a fast car that didn’t even wear a Racing Bull badge.
Unless you’ve been living under a rock for your entire life or simply have had no interest whatsoever in automotive trivia, the story of how the Sant’Agata Bolognese brand was founded is one of the most common pieces of Italian supercar lore.
To refresh your memory, the story goes that Ferrucio Lamborghini, who was a wealthy tractor manufacturer, constantly complained to Enzo Ferrari about the poor quality of the clutches in the Ferraris he owned. Severely irritated, Enzo allegedly told Ferruccio to stick to tractors. Instead, Lamborghini started his own car company in 1963.
Three years later, Lamborghini Automobili unleashed the Miura, the mid-engine V12 that more or less invented the modern supercar. Then came the incredible Countach, the Diablo, the Murcielago, Aventador, and recently the Revuelto. With a few exceptions, mostly because of regulations, each of them has been wider, louder, and always faster than its predecessor.
These are the Lamborghinis of bedroom posters, but they aren’t the only cars that made the company what it is today. You see, for the better part of its first three decades of existence, Lamborghini was small potatoes far from what it represents now, as it was always short of money and regularly close to collapse.
Its ownership changed hands several times, with Ferruccio himself selling his majority stake in 1972 and leaving the automotive industry altogether in 1974. The company he left even went bankrupt at the end of 1978. Obviously, with all these conundrums happening constantly, a company couldn’t pull through on selling V12 flagships alone.
To survive, Lamborghini eventually needed to make less expensive cars as well, or cars that suit the tax or emissions rules in certain markets, and sometimes even cars that make sense to almost no one outside Sant’Agata Bolognese.
As it happens, some of those “other Lamborghinis” were slow, albeit not in the traditional “0 to 60 in eventually” slow. They were definitely sluggish in the context of having the same badge as a 200-mph, mid-engine V12 Lambo, though. Don’t get me wrong, a Lamborghini that takes more than 7 seconds to reach 100 kph (62 mph), or begins to run out of breath short of reaching 250 kph (155 mph) doesn’t seem so deserving of the Raging Bull badge, yet a few of them have existed.
In other words, just like with other similar carmakers, like Ferrari, not everything that came out wearing a Lambo badge has been the fastest thing on four wheels during its era. On top of it, not all “slow” Lamborghinis have been entry level models either. The following shortlist of “lethargic Lambos" comprises all sorts of cars, from V12-powered grand tourers to V8 baby Lambos and there is even a V12 off-roader originally made for the military.
Lamborghini 400 GT 2+2: The Gentleman’s Private Express Train, Upstaged at its Own Debut The 400 GT in 2+2 guise had the bad luck of being introduced to the world at the 1966 Geneva Motor Show, which was the same venue where Lamborghini also unveiled the Miura P400. This was definitely a planned but terrible coincidence, because one was a mid-engined sensation that changed how fast cars should be made and the other was essentially a taller 350 GT with two extra seats.
Proportionally, the majority of people praised the Miura over the 400 GT 2+2, but it’s the front-engined V12 that Ferrucio actually wanted to build all along. Despite how the most successful Lambos ever ended up being like, he was more of a fan of reasonably fast, quiet, and comfortable grand tourers.
Photo: RM Sotheby's The 400 GT 2+2 did tick a lot of boxes in its segment. Its Bizzarrini-designed V12 was enlarged to 3.9 liters compared to its predecessor and developed 320 PS (316 HP) and 374 Nm (276 lb-ft) of torque, fed by no less than six twin-choke Weber carburetors. Lamborghini also replaced the earlier ZF gearbox with a five-speed of its own design, while also adding a limited-slip differential.
Despite room for two (small) passengers), the wheelbase was identical with the 350 GT, with the two extra seats being carved out of the existing cabin by slightly raising the roofline and reshaping the floor. That said, it was slightly heavier than its predecessors, which made it a bit slower.
With a 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) acceleration time of around 7.5 seconds and a top speed of around 250 kph (155 mph), the 400 GT 2+2 was no slouch for the era, but in the context of the Miura sharing its stage it felt like a snail. In other words, the long-hooded grand tourer belongs on this list more as a marker than an actual culprit, but it was still the slowest Lamborghini of its day.
Lamborghini Islero and Espada: Ferruccio’s Favorites, Yet the Ones Nobody Took to the Autostrada Named after the bull that killed famous matador Manolete, the Islero is arguably the second-fiercest name for a Lamborghini after the Diablo. It arrived at the 1968 Geneva Motor Show as a replacement for the 400 GT 2+2, where it shared the stand with the Espada, which was named after the sword used by matadors to kill the bull.
Like its predecessor, which was upstaged by the Miura, the Islero caught almost no one’s attention compared to the Espada, which was a true four-seater that looked a lot more dramatic. One reason could have been that the more traditional-looking (apart from its funky popup headlights) Islero had been designed by Mario Marazzi, while the Espada was the work of legendary Marcello Gandini. The Espada also broke a lot of norms regarding the exterior design of a grand tourer.
Photo: Lamborghini Both cars were powered by the same Bizzarrini V12, which sent a similar amount of power as their 400 GT 2+2 predecessors to the rear wheels through a Lamborghini-designed 5-speed manual transmission. The Espada was larger and much heavier, closer to an American-style grand tourer, and it also offered a 3-speed automatic transmission as an option.
With no update regarding their outputs and increased weight, both the Islero but especially the Jarama were not exactly quicker, nor faster than the cars they replaced, making for a pretty peculiar Lamborghini duo. A year later, Lamborghini did introduce the Islero S, which came with 350 horsepower, bigger brakes and a revised rear suspension, also increasing its top speed to about 260 kph (161 mph), while the 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) time dropped to 6.2 seconds.
Those numbers didn’t help much, as the Islero only lasted for about 14 months as part of the lineup, leaving everyone except Ferruccio underwhelmed. It is said that the company’s founder used one as his personal car, as did his brother Edmondo, but overall it was too discreet in both sales and performance, and the Espada wasn’t much of an improvement in that regard either.
Lamborghini Jarama 400 GT: More Power, More Weight, But No More Speed The Jarama was Lamborghini’s third attempt at the same idea in about five years. Like the 400 GT 2+@ and the Islero before it, it was a front-engined V12 coupe with two small rear seats. The somewhat unusual explanation for its existence in the first place was that the Islero would have needed a major redesign to meet new American safety and emission rules, so Lamborghini simply decided to start from scratch.
Well, almost from scratch since the Jarama was actually based on a shortened version of the Espada platform, with which it shared its engine and transmission(s). Presented at the Geneva Motor Show in 1970, it was designed by long-time collaborator Marcello Gandini. Gandini gave it a wide, somewhat blunt-looking and angular body, with half-exposed headlights, which was a very different and more flamboyant look compared to the more restrained and traditional-looking Islero.
Photo: RM Sotheby's The Jarama’s wheelbase was not only shorter than the Espada’s but it was even smaller than that of the Islero, making for the most compact 2+2 in Lamborghini’s lineup. Despite the coincidence, its name wasn’t a tribute to the Spanish racing circuit but actually referred to the Jarama region in Spain, known for breeding fighting bulls.
Its engine was the familiar Bizzarrini design V12 with 6 Weber carburettors, albeit it was now rated at 350 horsepower and a healthy 392 Nm (289 lb-ft) of torque. While being 30 horsepower more powerful than the Islero, the smaller Jarama was actually about 150 kg (330 pounds) heavier. In other words, the extra power and the extra mass pretty much cancelled each other out, with its top speed revolving around the 245 kph (161 mph) mark, while the 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) acceleration took over 7 seconds.
Despite, once again, being one of Ferruccio’s favorites, with a later-model Jarama S S being once again his personal car, not many other people shared this view. In fact, almost everyone thought it was too slow, especially for a Lamborghini, and in some ways you could say they were right.
Lamborghini Urraco P111: The Baby Lamborghini That Arrived in the U.S. Short of 40 Horsepower The Urraco was supposed to be the car that would transform Lamborghini from a boutique to a volume sports carmaker. It was a compact 2+2 with a mid-mounted V8, and it was once again styled by Marcello Gandini at Bertone. The model was aimed to disturb the party held by cars like the Porsche 911, Ferrari Dino, or the Maserati Merak.
Shown at the Turin Motor Show in 1970, it took another two years for production to begin and first customers didn’t get their cars until 1973, by which time the oil crisis was in full swing and Lamborghini was slowly sliding toward bankruptcy. From the start, the U.S. was supposed to be the Urraco's biggest market, but getting there meant meeting federal safety and emission laws.
Photo: RM Sotheby's To prepare it, Lamborghini swapped its Weber carburetors for Solex units and bolted on those dreadful-looking impact bumpers, completely changing both its specs and its looks for the worse. Power for the 2.5-liter V8 used fell from 220 PS (217 HP) to around 180 PS (177 HP), which was even less than the 2.0-liter Urraco P200 that Lamborghini sold at home to get around Italy’s 38 percent tax on engines larger than 2.0 liters.
The European Urraco P250 was good for 240 kph (149 mph), with 100 kph (62 mph) coming up in 6.9 seconds. The American-only P111 barely managed 215 kph (134 mph), while the 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) took almost 10 seconds.
It was simply the slowest Lamborghini ever produced up to that point, and with an exterior look that only a mother would love, it's no wonder that only 21 units were ever built and sold. To put things into perspective, a Corvette Stingray 454 from 1974 would hit 100 kph (62 mph) in under 6 seconds, making it almost twice as quick as the twice as expensive baby Lambo.
Lamborghini LM002: By Far, the Slowest V12 Lamborghini Ever Each of the cars on this list were slow mainly because they had too little power for the Lamborghini badge, especially when it comes to the Urraco P111. On the other hand, the LM002 had 450 horsepower, which is obviously more than anything else, and by a wide margin.
In short, its lackluster on-road performance was obviously not for a lack of power, but for weighing about 2,700 kg (5,952 pounds) and having the drag coefficient of a small building. The “Rambo Lambo,” as it was affectionately nicknamed, had started as a military project, with Lamborghini building a prototype called the Cheetah.
While the original was powered by a rear-mounted Chrysler V8, the next two versions were upgraded to a front-mounted Lamborghini V12, or exactly the same engine used in the Countach, to be more precise.
Photo: Lamborghini The name LM002 came from “Lamborghini Militaria, second prototype,” although it was the third if we also take into account the Cheetah. The civilian production version was unveiled at the Brussels Motor Show in 1986, and its specifications list sounded a bit like a dream. The 5.2-liter V12 developed 450 horsepower and 500 Nm (369 lb-ft) of torque, sent to all four wheels through a 5-speed manual and a two-speed transfer case.
In short, it was the most powerful and arguably the most brutal-looking off-roader on the planet. Its tires were developed by Pirelli specifically for the LM002 and used run-flat technology. As you would expect, fuel consumption was not its strong point, with 30 to 35 liters per 100 km (7 to 8 mpg US) being common, which is probably why Lamborghini fitted it with a 169-liter (45 gallons) fuel tank.
Then again, nobody bought a Lamborghini expecting it to sip fuel like a family car, but its on-road performance was not exactly stellar either. As a matter of fact, it is by far the slowest road-going Lamborghini in history, and its record will probably never be beaten.
While it was quicker than an Urraco from 0 to 100 kph (62 mph), the LM002’s weight and brick-shaped aerodynamics gave it a top speed of just 210 kph (130 mph). On the other hand, it’s also the only production Lamborghini that could climb 120-degree gradients, thus also making it the quickest thoroughbred off-roader of its time.
